newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - AUSTRALIAN Q2 FINAL WAGES DATA.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - AUSTRALIAN Q2 FINAL WAGES DATA.

text.p: Australian private sector average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) fell by 0.1 percent in the three months to May to be 2.5 percent higher over the year, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.

Private sector AWOTE had grown by 3.6 percent in the year to February. Public sector AWOTE rose by 1.6 percent in the quarter to be up 7.2 percent over the year. Public sector wages had grown by 7.1 percent in the year to February.
Preliminary AWOTE for the quarter were revised to 0.3 percent from the 0.5 percent published in July.
Annual growth was revised to 3.5 percent. A selection of analysts' initial reaction to the data follows:
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It's obviously a very inflation friendly result and suggests that we're going to keep inflation at very low levels for the next year or so. It might make you a little more comfortable about inflation in the second half of 1998, which I think is the key to whether there'll be another rate cut or not. But our view is still that monetary policy is hold for the forseeable future."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"We haven't seen a number as low as that for many years and the composition is also very strong for markets. The negative growth in private ... is a very good outcome. But I have to say we query the reliability of those numbers. Our own HSBC Markets wages report is showing some acceleration in enterprise bargaining outcomes and we know that minimum wages are increasing at much the same rate as they have over the last couple of years. It is difficult to find a reason for such an exceptionally low number."
NIGEL DOUGLAS, FIXED INCOME STRATEGIST, MERRILL LYNCH:

"The revisions were downward, better than expected and private sector earnings dropping 0.1 percent shows that wages are not a problem. But, the big jump in public sector may raise the question of compositional changes, so data is analysed closely."
PETER MUNCKTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"They were clearly very good. The wages position is even better than the most optimistic market expectations, so clearly inflation is not going to be a concern for the RBA. If they're unhappy with the activity front, they've got room to cut rates."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"It's an encouraging result. I'm not so sure private sector wages are falling. Taking the average of 3.5 (percent), it is so far away from the RBA danger level that it has to be encouraging. If there are arguments for an easing, then these figures certainly don't work against it. Non-inflationary type wages growth is good to see."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"The key number from a policy prospective is private wages and the public will lag what is going on in the private sector. It is a very sharp decelaration in private sector wages. The minus you can't believe. It is consistent with underlying inflation staying lower in the next year. It is a very encouraging result for the Reserve Bank and by itself it has to increase the chances, or certainly leaves more room to contemplate another easing in policy in late October."
TONY MEER, ECONOMIST, DEUTCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"The first thing you notice is that it's the second quarter in a row in which we have had a downward revision between the preliminary and the final, so what that does suggest is that the ABS has been very conservative in the approximation taken from the survey. The second thing you notice is a fall in private sector earnings down 0.1 percent. It does seem a little implausible, if you look at the industry composition most of the industries are doing more or less then what you would expect them to be doing, around four percent plus, except property and businesses."
